title: Higher cellular competency accelerates evolutionary search in a 1D embryo model

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Higher cellular competency accelerates evolutionary search in a 1D embryo model

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In a minimal artificial embryogeny model (1D integer arrays whose fitness is their monotonicity, with competent cells performing a restricted bubble sort before fitness evaluation), populations with higher cellular competency reached high fitness faster and more consistently than hardwired populations, e.g. under 6 generations at competency 400 versus over 200 for hardwired.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Shreesha L 2023, Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model › 3. Results › 3.2. Developmental Competency Accelerates Evolutionary Search

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: These data demonstrate the role competency plays in non-linearly improving the rate of fitness of a population and support a clear conclusion: the higher the competency, the better the performance.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Shreesha L, Levin M, “Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model”, Entropy (Basel, Switzerland) (2023), doi:10.3390/e25010131; section “3. Results › 3.2. Developmental Competency Accelerates Evolutionary Search”. Scope: In silico 1D artificial embryos evolved with a genetic algorithm

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2023-competency-04: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.88

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The model, fitness function, and competency operation are simple and publicly specified. A small team can independently implement and rerun the experiment.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reimplement the specified genetic algorithm and restricted bubble sort, run repeated populations at each competency, and compare generations to fitness thresholds. The under-6 versus over-200 generation contrast is directly falsifiable.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The result applies only to the toy fitness landscape.

Exact random seeds and implementation details may be unavailable.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.96
data existence: 0.72

analysis feasibility: 0.92

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fitness is an explicit inversion count, competency is a bounded bubble-sort, and the competent-versus-hardwired experiment is a public script with hyperparameters. A small team can rerun it in days to weeks and compare time-to-fitness. The claim is about this model, and the code covers that scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Rerun the public 1D embryogeny experiment at the published competency levels, including 400, and at the hardwired setting, and record generations until high phenotypic fitness. Competent populations reaching that fitness faster and more consistently, on the order of under 6 generations versus over 200, would confirm the claim; overlapping times would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Exact generation counts depend on the published mutation rate, selection stringency and fitness definition.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.95
data adequacy: 0.88
data existence: 0.9
discriminating power: 0.82
analysis feasibility: 0.78

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: In an independent re-implementation of the Shreesha & Levin (2023) artificial-embryogeny genetic algorithm, the best individual's phenotypic fitness (mean over repeats) crosses each fitness threshold sooner the higher the competency level, with competency 400 reaching fitness 1.0 within a few generations and the hardwired population taking far longer.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py re-implements the model in vectorised numpy without importing the authors' code: per generation it records the best genotypic fitness, develops each embryo by restricted bubble sort, selects the top 10 on phenotypic fitness, refills to 100 by single-point crossover and point-mutates each individual with probability 0.6. Hardwired and competency 20, 100 and 400 populations are each run 100 times for 250 generations from fixed seeds. For each Table 1 threshold it reports the first generation at which the mean best phenotypic fitness reaches it, and runs one-sided Welch t-tests of each competent population against hardwired at generations 2, 10 and 20.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: with 100 repeats of 250 generations per condition, (a) the generation at which the mean best phenotypic fitness first reaches 1.0 is strictly ordered hardwired > competency 20 > competency 100 > competency 400, and the same weak ordering (>=) holds at every Table 1 threshold (0.65, 0.75, 0.8, 0.9, 0.97, 1.0); (b) competency 400 reaches 1.0 by generation 10 and hardwired does not reach it before generation 100; (c) at generations 2, 10 and 20 each competent population's best phenotypic fitness exceeds hardwired with Welch t-test p < 0.001.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: at the 0.97 or 1.0 threshold some higher competency level is strictly slower than a lower one (including hardwired faster than any competent level), or a competent population is not better than hardwired at generation 10 (p >= 0.05 or lower mean). Outcomes meeting neither the pass nor the fail criterion (ordering holds but the magnitudes in (b) or the significance in (c) are not met) are pre-registered as 'mixed'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: generations for the mean best phenotypic fitness of the competency-400 population to reach 1.0

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: Monte Carlo; fixed seed, deterministic for a given numpy version

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: This is a simulation-result claim, so the test is replication: re-run the described model and check that the reported dynamics follow from it. Parameters are taken from Supplement S1/S2.1 of the paper (array of 50 cells, values 1-50 drawn with repetition, 100 embryos, top 10% selected on phenotypic fitness, crossover, per-individual point-mutation probability 0.6, competency levels 20/100/400) and unspecified details from the authors' code (github.com/Niwhskal/CellularCompetency, commit 2be29f96): fitness 9^x/9 where x is the normalized non-inversion count; restricted bubble sort that swaps strictly inverted adjacent pairs, visiting positions in a fresh random order each sweep, up to the competency limit; selected parents are kept and children are added by single-point crossover (cut in [11, 50)) until the population is refilled, then every individual is point-mutated with probability 0.6. 'Reaches a threshold' follows the paper's Table 1: the first generation at which the mean over repeats of the best individual's fitness is >= the threshold. The re-implementation is written independently (vectorised numpy) and does not import the authors' code.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Re-implementation of Shreesha & Levin (2023) Experiment 1, 100 repeats x 250 generations x 4 populations (generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
This is a replication of a simulation, not an empirical test: it shows the reported dynamics follow from the stated model, not that real cellular competency accelerates evolution.

All pre-registered criteria hold: strict ordering at fitness 1.0 (230 > 72 > 33 > 4 generations), weak ordering at every threshold, competency 400 at 1.0 by generation 4, hardwired after generation 100, and every Welch test p < 1e-10.

The re-run is consistently somewhat faster than Table 1 (e.g. competency 20 reaches 1.0 at 72 vs 93, hardwired at 230 vs 250). The authors' plotting code counts hardwired crossings from 0 and competent crossings from 1, and their committed configuration uses 10 repeats rather than the 100 stated in the supplement; either could account for small offsets. The qualitative claim does not depend on them.

'Under 6 generations at competency 400' is reproduced (4); the claim's 'over 200 for hardwired' is reproduced (230), but that number is sensitive to the 1.0 threshold, which requires every one of the 100 repeats to be perfectly sorted in the same generation.

Genotypic fitness plateaus lower the higher the competency (0.97, 0.87 and 0.59 at generation 250 vs 1.0 hardwired), consistent with the companion claim levin-2023-competency-05; that claim is not tested here.
